title: The Library of Alexandria never burned
premise: In 48 BCE the harbor fire in Alexandria is stopped before it reaches the book stores. The Library keeps its catalogs, workshops and copy trade. Learning stays linked to crafts and trade, so steam, rail and electric systems appear centuries early.

chain.event: A fire starting among harbor store sheds in Alexandria is stopped by harbor workers with water buckets and cleared sheds before it reaches the book stores.
chain.consequence: The rolls, catalogs and copying rooms stay in use, and duplicate copies continue to be sold and shipped to other ports.

chain.event: Copy workshops in Alexandria and other eastern Mediterranean ports sell standardized star tables, maps and mechanical calendars made with water-powered lathes and screw presses.
chain.consequence: Shipowners and surveyors buy them in volume, creating steady income for instrument makers and schools that train measurers and copyists.

chain.event: Improved bellows furnaces and expanded charcoal and coal shipments allow workshops in Egypt and the Levant to cast thicker iron cylinders and boilers.
chain.consequence: Piston pumps and small coal-fed steam pumps come into regular use to drain mines and lift water for mills and gardens.

chain.event: Millwrights combine iron boilers with piston, crank and flywheel to build low-pressure stationary steam engines for flour mills, oil presses and textile shops.
chain.consequence: Mill districts expand and bulk flour, oil, cloth and paper become cheaper, supporting larger towns and wider trade in grain and coal.

chain.event: Mine rail lines with iron rails are extended between coal pits, ports and cities with steam locomotives, while distilled coal gas is piped to street lamps and workshops.
chain.consequence: Freight costs fall sharply, suburbs grow around stations, and evening work and travel become common in large cities.

chain.event: Fine wire drawing, acid and glass trades allow production of dynamos, batteries and incandescent lamps funded by railway and shipping profits.
chain.consequence: Electric streetcars, wired telegraph and telephone exchanges, and factory lighting spread, raising urban density and office work.

chain.event: Experimenters using vacuum tubes and calculation engines build long-distance radio and early programmable calculating machines for rail, bank and weather offices.
chain.consequence: Automated control spreads to power grids and factories, allowing taller buildings with lifts, air handling and electric transit by the early 1900s.

eras.caption: 26 CE · The Library stands; far away, little has changed yet
eras.visualPrompt: Transform this scene to 26 CE in a world where the Library of Alexandria never burned. Only seventy years after the change, places far from the Mediterranean look as they did in our history; around the Mediterranean, towns are a little denser, better paved and better watered.
eras.visualPromptIndoor: Interior of a copy room with long wooden tables, stacked paper sheets, ink jars and shelves of scroll rolls lit by daylight from small windows.

differences: around the Mediterranean only: slightly denser two-storey town houses instead of single-storey ones (because copying and trade income starts to grow towns)
around the Mediterranean only: paved main streets with covered drains instead of dirt lanes (because Alexandrian engineering manuals spread along sea routes)
around the Mediterranean only: waterwheels and screw pumps at the town edge instead of rope wells (because mechanics notes reach millwrights)
everywhere else: exactly as in our history at this date (because the change has had only seventy years to travel)
kept: the region’s own building tradition and way of life outside the Mediterranean

eras.visualPromptIndoor: Interior of a gaslit print and reading room with iron stoves, paper presses, glass lamp shades and rows of tables with books and timetables.

differences: Four- to six-story brick tenements and workshops instead of one- to two-story timber and stone houses (because steam-powered brickworks, iron beams and rail freight support taller rental blocks)
Rail lines with steam locomotives and station yards instead of horse tracks and coaching inns (because coal-fed traction carries bulk grain and cloth between cities)
Piped gas street lamps and lit shop windows instead of torches and shuttered stalls (because coal-gas mains light evening streets and extend shop hours)
Wide paved avenues with sidewalks and iron drains instead of muddy lanes with central gutters (because taxes on mill and rail trade pay for road crews)
Printed paper signs, timetables and price lists instead of painted wooden boards (because steam presses produce cheap paper in volume)
kept: courtyard patterns in the region's own tradition

eras.caption: 1926 · Tall towers and electric trams
eras.visualPrompt: Transform this scene to 1926 in a world where the library of alexandria never burned. Show tall steel-frame towers in the region's own building tradition, electric trams and delivery vans, buried-cable streetlights and illuminated signs.
eras.visualPromptIndoor: Interior of an electric office with ceiling lights, desk telephones, calculating machines, metal filing cabinets and large windows.

differences: Twenty-story steel-frame towers in dense centers instead of four-story brick blocks (because electric lifts and air handling make tall offices and flats practical)
Battery trams and electric delivery vans on asphalt lanes instead of steam trains and early hand-cranked cars (because city power grids and storage cells support quiet street transit)
Buried power cables and bright electric streetlights instead of overhead tram wires and gas lamps (because underground mains feed lights and transit reliably)
Illuminated display panels and clock timetables instead of painted wooden billboards (because electric signs and standard time sustain evening shopping and commuting)
Paved sidewalks with planted trees and piped drains instead of cobble streets with open gutters (because power and water income pays for street planting and sewers)
kept: terrain and harbor or river shape
street trees and local garden plants

eras.caption: 2026 · Garden towers and pod transit
eras.visualPrompt: Transform this scene to 2026 in a world where the library of alexandria never burned. Show slender garden towers in the region's own building tradition, automated pods on reserved lanes, solar canopies and planted rain gardens.
eras.visualPromptIndoor: Interior of a bright living and work room with garden balcony, adjustable daylight panels, wall display for transit and weather, and quiet electric heating and cooling.

differences: Slender forty-story towers with garden terraces instead of ten-story concrete slabs (because lightweight frames, fast lifts and balanced grids make tall green housing routine)
Automated electric pods on reserved lanes and aerial cable cabins instead of privately owned gasoline cars (because fleet transit and grid power lower street noise and parking needs)
Rooftop plantings and solar canopies with buried grids instead of tar roofs and overhead power lines (because building codes link power production to roof gardens)
Low-energy text panels and wayfinding lights instead of large paper billboards and neon signs (because networked displays update transit and shop information instantly)
Permeable paving with rain gardens and cycle tracks instead of wide asphalt lots (because stormwater rules and fleet transit reduce paved parking)
kept: the region's own courtyard and roof patterns

eras.caption: 2126 · Towers far beyond ours, quiet streets below
eras.visualPrompt: Transform this scene to 2126 in a world where the Library of Alexandria never burned, eight centuries ahead of ours. Very tall slender towers of pale stone and glass with planted terraces rise far above the photo's skyline, with wide quiet streets, silent trams and fountains below.
eras.visualPromptIndoor: This room in 2126 eight centuries ahead: pale stone, a full-height window looking out over a city of slender towers, a wall of books.

differences: slender towers of a hundred storeys and more instead of mid-rise buildings (because structural engineering is centuries ahead)
wide quiet streets with silent trams and no traffic jams instead of car roads (because transport was solved long ago)
pale stone, glass and planted terraces on towers instead of concrete and asphalt (because building materials matured over centuries)
great libraries and observatories as landmarks instead of shopping centres (because the city grew around learning)

eras.caption: 3026 · Parkland over a city that went underground
eras.visualPrompt: Transform this scene to 3026 in a world where the Library of Alexandria never burned. Most of the city has moved below ground: the surface is open parkland, meadows and woods, with only a few slender pale towers, skylights and garden domes rising from it.
eras.visualPromptIndoor: This room in 3026 eight centuries ahead: a calm underground hall lit by a skylight from the park above.

differences: open parkland and woods at the surface instead of streets and buildings (because the city's homes and transport moved underground)
a few slender pale towers and glass skylights instead of a skyline of blocks (because only landmarks stay above ground)
meadows and streams instead of paved squares (because the surface is given back to nature)
